questions.q: What table does the System Log application's "All" and "Errors" views sit on top of?
questions.explain: The System Log application's modules are filtered views over the syslog table.

questions.q: Which System Log view shows web request-level logging, useful for chasing a performance problem or confirming a request reached the server?
questions.explain: System Log > Transactions shows individual web request-level log entries.

questions.q: What are the three real script-level calls that write a message into the log, in order of increasing severity?
questions.explain: gs.info(), gs.warn(), and gs.error() are the real script-level logging calls, at increasing severity.

questions.q: Why is the System Log described as the primary tool for the troubleshooting workflow introduced in Chapter 2's access-denied lesson?
options: It only logs ACL-related denials and nothing else
It makes a much wider range of problems visible, including script failures and integration errors, not just ACL issues
It replaces the need to understand how ACLs evaluate access
It is only useful for Scheduled Job troubleshooting
questions.explain: The System Log surfaces evidence for many kinds of failures beyond ACL denials, making it the broader troubleshooting tool.

questions.q: What is the real, repeatable admin workflow for finding relevant log entries in a table that can hold thousands of unrelated rows?
options: Scroll through System Log > All from the newest entry until something looks relevant
Reproduce the issue, note the timestamp, then check the relevant log view around that timestamp
Delete old log entries first so only recent ones remain
Ask the vendor to search the log on your behalf
questions.explain: Reproducing the issue and anchoring the search to that timestamp is what makes the log searchable instead of overwhelming.
